tables.how: Every line of the departments’ gift reports on file (1,933 lines, $39,709,059); 7 lines that are the form’s blank template (donor “Name is required.”) are left out, as in the analysis. “Tied” marks the 93 donor-and-department pairs the next list sets out: a contract, grant, permit or lease written on the form, or the same department paying a payee of the same name $5,000 or more in fiscal 2025 to 2027.
tables.limits: Giving to a department must be reported exactly like this and is often simple generosity. Individual donors are not named, as the analysis does not name them: a gift report can name a patient’s family or a member of the public (1,048 donors are counted this way). When a department amends a month the list keeps only the latest filing’s lines, so 53 earlier filings have no lines here.

tables.how: From the side-doors analysis: a donor is listed when the department wrote a contract, licence, permit or other financial tie on the form, or the payment file shows the same department paying a payee of the same name $5,000 or more in fiscal 2025 to 2027. 93 organizations, $6,381,842 in gifts; for 14 a contract with that department began within 365 days of a gift.
tables.limits: Most ties are the ordinary relationship between a department and the organizations built around it: resident arts companies, a hospital foundation, a grantee donating to an event. A gift near a contract date is a coincidence in time, not evidence that one caused the other; many of these contracts were competitively bid. Donor and payee are matched by name.

tables.how: From the side-doors analysis: Form 700 filers with a seat on a board or commission (1,332 people). Their Schedule A-2 entries (businesses owned 10% or more) and Schedule C entries with a stated position or income of $10,000 or more are matched by name to the City’s payment file, payments summed for the fiscal years overlapping the years declared, and kept at $25,000 or more: 194 pairs, 21 paid by the member’s own department ($103,187,359). Stock holdings (Schedule A-1) are counted only (577 pairs) and not listed.
tables.limits: Commissioners are appointed because they work in the field, and many seats are reserved for people from funded or regulated organizations. The rule is that a member takes no part in a decision affecting the source; payments are by department, not by decision, so nothing here shows a payment came before the member. A common business name can be a different firm.

tables.limits: The minutes print surnames only, so two members with one surname on one body would be joined. A missing notice may be a notice filed under another spelling or date, or one not required for that kind of recusal.

tables.how: From the officials analysis: every approved appointment of a person (not a supervisor) to a body in a Board file from 2015, one row per person, body and authority: 1,197 (890 Board of Supervisors, 237 Mayor, 29 President of the Board of Supervisors, 25 not printed, 12 Treasurer, 4 Controller). The analysis also looks each appointee up by name among donors to the appointing official: of 174 mayoral appointees with a rare name, 55 share it with a donor to the appointing mayor and 49 with a donor to a different mayor. Those name matches are not shown person by person, because a name alone does not make two records one person; the last column marks only the appointees the analysis ties by a second link (an occupation of commissioner on the contribution, or an employer that is an income source on the appointee’s own Form 700).
tables.limits: Appointees are often active in civic life and give to campaigns for their own reasons; the comparison with donors to a different mayor shows how politically active appointees are in general. Commissions the Mayor fills without a Board file appear only through their own member pages, and rosters before 2025 are not on disk.

tables.limits: A seat filled before 2015, or by a Mayor without a Board file, has no appointing official on disk. Being appointed by a Mayor is the ordinary way these seats are filled.

sources.t: San Francisco Ethics Commission: Enforcement Penalties Issued (DataSF)

tables.how: Every record in the Commission’s penalty file (164 penalties, $1,011,424), with the analysis’s reading of the year of the events and of the largest sum the stipulation describes. 13 are for not filing the yearly statement of economic interests ($33,945).
tables.limits: A penalty is a civil settlement or order, not a criminal finding. The sum read from a stipulation is often the size of the campaign or contract around the case, not the amount at issue, so the words beside it are printed. The year of the events is an estimate.

tables.limits: A late statement is a filing lapse, usually closed after a reminder; most are days or weeks late. The statement is due April 1; April 10 is used because that is when the first non-filer list is drawn up.
